data.title: Antimalarials: hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, quinacrine
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Immunomodulators_

**Class:** 4-aminoquinolines (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine) and acridine (quinacrine/mepacrine)

## Mechanism of action
- Weak bases that accumulate in lysosomes and raise their pH → impaired antigen processing and MHC-II presentation
- Inhibit endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR7, TLR9) → less type I interferon (key in lupus)
- Absorb UV light, bind melanin, stabilise membranes; mild anti-platelet and lipid/glucose-lowering effects
- In porphyria cutanea tarda: form water-soluble complexes with porphyrins in the liver that are excreted in urine

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; huge volume of distribution; very long half-life (40–50 days) → takes 2–3 months to work
- Bound to melanin (skin, retina) — basis of retinopathy and pigmentation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous lupus (DLE, SCLE) and SLE (first-line; reduces flares and thrombosis)
- Dermatomyositis skin disease, Sjögren, rheumatoid arthritis
- Photodermatoses: polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria (adjunct), lymphocytic infiltrate of Jessner
- Porphyria cutanea tarda — low dose (HCQ 100 mg or chloroquine 125 mg twice weekly)
- Others: lichen planopilaris and frontal fibrosing alopecia, morphoea, sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, chronic urticaria (refractory), oral lichen planus
- Quinacrine: added to HCQ in refractory cutaneous lupus (no retinal toxicity)

## Dose & formulations
- Hydroxychloroquine: ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day (usually 200–400 mg/day)
- Chloroquine: ≤2.3 mg/kg real body weight/day (usually 250 mg/day)
- Quinacrine: 100 mg/day
- Never combine HCQ with chloroquine (additive retinal toxicity)

## Adverse effects
- Retinopathy ('bull's-eye' maculopathy) — related to daily dose per kg and duration; risk higher with chloroquine, renal disease, tamoxifen
- Skin: blue-grey/black pigmentation (shins, face, palate, nails), bleaching of hair (chloroquine), exacerbation of psoriasis, AGEP (HCQ is a classic cause), SJS/TEN, lichenoid eruptions
- Quinacrine: diffuse yellow skin discolouration, aplastic anaemia (rare)
- GI upset, headache; myopathy and cardiomyopathy (long-term); haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; hypoglycaemia; QT prolongation
- Accidental overdose in children is often fatal (chloroquine)

## Contraindications
- Pre-existing maculopathy; hypersensitivity; caution in psoriasis, G6PD deficiency, porphyria (except low-dose regimen), epilepsy, long QT

## Drug interactions
- Tamoxifen (retinopathy risk), QT-prolonging drugs, digoxin (levels rise), antacids (separate by 4 h), cyclosporine levels rise, smoking reduces efficacy in lupus

## Monitoring
- Baseline eye examination (fundus) within the first year; annual screening (OCT and visual fields) after 5 years on HCQ (earlier with risk factors)
- CBC and LFT periodically

## Pregnancy & lactation
Hydroxychloroquine is safe and recommended to continue in pregnancy (reduces lupus flares, congenital heart block risk in anti-Ro mothers); compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Mechanism: lysosomal pH, TLR7/9 inhibition
- Dose by real body weight: HCQ ≤5 mg/kg, chloroquine ≤2.3 mg/kg
- Bull's-eye maculopathy; AGEP; psoriasis flare
- Low-dose twice-weekly regimen in porphyria cutanea tarda
- Smoking reduces response in cutaneous lupus

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.21 (Antimalarial agents); Khopkar (Antimalarials in LE and porphyria cutanea tarda). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
